title_en: Burnham in Brussels: why party politics still defines the UK’s relationship with Europe
excerpt_en: The talks were part of a UK-EU ‘reset’.
body_en: Andy Burnham has attended his first EU-UK summit in Brussels with major agreements reached on youth mobility, food exports and carbon emissions. Ultimately though, the prime minister will have understood that this was merely the start of new political negotiations. Back home in the UK, he has started a “national conversation” on the future of UK-EU relations that gained momentum rapidly.

Burnham held talks with European Council president Antonio Costa and president of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen. Both Burnham and Costa come from sister social democratic parties and both are former mayors – Burnham of Greater Manchester and Costa of Lisbon. This could make for smoother meetings in future than in the months and years after the 2016 Brexit referendum.

In the run up to the talks, the prime minister had repeatedly claimed that the Conservatives failed to get a good deal from the EU. As part of former prime minister Keir Starmer’s “reset” of relations with Europe, then-business secretary, Peter Kyle, and European Commission vice-president Teresa Ribera signed a deal committing the UK and the EU to closer cooperation on trade.

Like Costa and Burnham, Ribera is also from a European social democratic party (the Spanish Socialist Workers Party, or PSOE). Senior figures in Labour have long admired the electoral success of social democrats in both Spain and Portugal.

When it comes to claims of the UK having had a bad deal, there is one explanation that is under-discussed. It has its roots in the internal party politics of the centre-right in Europe. Ahead of the 2009 European Parliament elections, the then-Conservative leader David Cameron decided to leave the European People’s Party (a bloc of centre-right pro-European parties).

Cameron went on to set up a new right-of-centre eurosceptic faction with parties from Poland and the Czech Republic. But he underestimated how hurt highly influential EU figures like German chancellor Angela Merkel were by the move. So when it came to negotiating a better deal with the EU ahead of the 2016 referendum, Merkel and other figures had not forgotten Cameron’s betrayal. As such, they felt disinclined to meet him half way.

Burnham is walking a fine line Youth mobility, migration, food exports and emissions are all important issues. But the broader discussion is increasingly about the politics around Brexit rather than the rights and wrongs of Brexit itself.

The UK is not going to rejoin the EU in the near future. Burnham even said when standing in the Makerfield byelection that first and foremost he wants to sort the consequences of Brexit rather than necessarily the outcome.

Now Burnham is increasingly focused on the claim that Brexit hasn’t worked for British voters – without saying it was completely wrong. He may understand that aiming to reverse Brexit in a binary way could simply open up new problems. It could even finish his premiership in the same way that it ended the tenures of multiple prime ministers before him.

In contrast, however, Burnham understands that he has the political capital to discuss the downsides of Brexit. For now, at least, he can do this in a way that is unlikely to result in much political damage to his government. While not completely without risk, he has calculated that the benefits of discussing Brexit outweigh any costs.

These costs could include the fragile “red wall” of Labour seats in northern England and the Midlands. The party knows all too well that this could flip to Reform UK the next time the country goes to the polls.

But those voters who have already moved to Reform are something of a sunk cost for Labour. For now, it seems Burnham sees more advantages in drawing voters away from the Liberal Democrats and the Greens than he sees disadvantages in alienating supporters of Reform. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch appears to be sensitive to the fact that many people disapprove of how the Tories handled Brexit – whether they voted Remain or Leave.
At the height of the Brexit chaos, however, Burnham was mayor of Greater Manchester and so can revisit the issue in a fresh way, untainted by the Westminister turbulence of that time.

His predecessor Starmer was frequently seen as being paralysed by caution. Burnham appears to know how to talk about difficult issues lightly and fluently – his own parliamentary seat overwhelmingly voted Leave in 2016.

He may or may not truly want to see the UK rejoin the EU at some point – he has sometimes sent out mixed signals on the issue. But he certainly has the firm aim of removing the toxicity from the issue and having a “national conversation”. To do this, the prime minister will have to consider how Westminster relates to Brussels as well as how it relates to constituencies like his own in Makerfield.

Martin Steven does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

title_en: French police officers found guilty of racist assault on black music producer
excerpt_en: Beating of Michel Zecler in 2020 sparked outrage over police brutality after it was caught on security cameras
body_en: Three French police officers who beat a black music producer they said was not wearing a face mask during the Covid pandemic have been found guilty of intentional, racist violence.

The brutal assault on Michel Zecler, now 47, was caught on security cameras in his building in 2020 and triggered outrage in France over police brutality. The trial this month was considered a turning point for the recognition of racist violence.
The officers were sentenced to between one and two years in prison, with additional years suspended. They were banned for life from serving in the police.

The officers had stopped Zecler outside his Paris music studio on 21 November 2020, accusing him of failing to wear a mandatory face mask. They pushed him into the entrance of his office and violently beat him in an assault recorded by his studio’s security cameras.

Zecler sustained about 30 punches and truncheon blows to the face and body over a five-minute period, according to the investigation. He was left with craniofacial trauma, a wound to the lip and scalp, and a complete rupture of his biceps tendon, leaving him unable to work for 45 days.

Zecler told the court the officers used a racist slur against him on several occasions during the beating. He said the attack had “completely devastated him” and had left a lasting physical and psychological impact.

The three officers, Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Pierre Plantier, 37, and Philippe Tondeux, 50, were found guilty of breaking into Zecler’s studio and committing intentional violence in a group. The judges decided racism was an aggravating factor in the attack.

The officers were also found guilty of forgery after they tried to cover up their actions by falsifying an official police report saying Zecler had been violent towards them. The police used that report to accuse Zecler of attacking them and trying to grab one of their weapons, but the video footage did not back up the claims, showing he was not violent.

The state prosecutor said that without the CCTV footage, the false police report on Zecler could have resulted in him being convicted of attacking a police officer in what would have been a serious miscarriage of justice.
The state prosecutor, who asked not to be named in the media, told the court the case had caused “immense harm to Michel Zecler but also to society as a whole”.
She said the officers had “betrayed” their uniform. She told the judges: “I ask you to believe Michel Zecler, to recognise him as a victim of these racist insults.”
The three police officers, who had not realised their attack was being recorded on security cameras, had apologised in court for beating Zecler, but denied racism.

Zecler’s lawyers and supporters said the trial had shone a spotlight on police violence in France, which victims and researchers say is systemic but authorities and law enforcement unions say is limited to isolated cases. Many members of the public who had come to support Zecler and watch the trial said it was an important moment in confronting institutionalised racism.

One of Zecler’s lawyers, Serge Money, said while summing up the case: “A verdict can force a society to really look at an injustice that up until now had been tolerated, minimised, and I dare to use the word: institutionalised.”
He said: “The Zecler trial is the trial of impunity, for all those who before him and after him will experience the same thing.”
Money told the court: “I want you to give voice to all those who didn’t have security cameras, and to all those who were not believed.”
Nine young performers who had been rehearsing in the basement at Zecler’s studio had been violently arrested when they came to assist Zecler.
Their lawyer, Seydi Ba, told the court that France needed to know how “police violence, lies and racism” would be considered by a court.

title_en: Nasdaq erases all 2026 gains as AI sell-off dampens Anthropic’s second day of trading
excerpt_en: The Nasdaq lost trillions in value, with the AI startup’s IPO failing to buoy it as investors question huge sums being poured into AI buildout
body_en: As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite erased all its gains for 2026 and closed down 5% from its value on 1 January. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed in correction territory.
Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a global sell-off in AI-linked companies, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq erased some $4tn in market value this week, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Shares in the frontier AI company behind the Claude chatbot, which floated in the US on Thursday, fell by 9% on Friday, ceding most of the gains from the biggest initial public offering in history. They dropped to $88.30, towards the $83 level at which Anthropic priced its stock market debut.
Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the firm began.

US technology stocks followed Anthropic down on Friday, with the memory chipmaker SanDisk falling 14% and rival Micron down 12%. Nvidia fell 14%, eliminating hundreds of billions of dollars in market cap.
Related: Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn?

Neil Wilson, a UK investor strategist at Saxo, said there was “just relentless selling in tech”. He warned: “Anthropic shares tumbled to take an $85 handle as the post-IPO euphoria gives way to the reality of a steep sell-off across the tech and AI space that shows no sign of easing just yet.”

Global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%.

The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation ⁠of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies.

In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.
European stock markets posted their biggest weekly loss since March 2025, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.9% on Friday. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low.
The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO.

Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm.

“The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp said.

Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI buildout.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.

“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”
Nvidia shares fell byafter California served the chip company with a subpoena as part of an investigation into whether its advanced semiconductors ended up in China.
Britain’s FTSE 100 share index dropped by 5.1% this week, its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.

Fears that US central bankers may raise interest rates to fight inflation have lifted the dollar to a 19-month high, and pushed down the gold price – with gold on track for its worst week since March.
Bitcoin hit its lowest level in four months, dropping below the $60,000 point for the first time since early July.

title_en: Cop31 talks go into overtime as debate rages over lack of fossil fuels in draft deal
excerpt_en: African ministers say they ‘didn’t come here to beg’, with civil society groups calling it the ‘worst Cop ever’
body_en: Crucial climate talks headed into overtime on the last official day of the Cop31 UN summit as countries continued to argue over a draft deal that was silent on fossil fuels, with a host of other contentious issues complicating negotiations.

Nearly 200 countries struggled to bridge their differences after two weeks of intense talks and impassioned speeches in Antalya, Turkey, about the effects of climate breakdown around the world, with a scheduled finish of Friday evening breached.
“At this point, no one is happy,” Brazil’s national secretary for climate change, Aloisio Lopes Pereira de Melo, told reporters.

The Guardian understands there will probably not be a new draft of an agreement for negotiators to pore over until Saturday morning. A sprawling initial draft deal released earlier this week included strong calls to accelerate the phase-out of coal, oil and gas, but a second, shorter version on Thursday did not include mention of fossil fuels and weakened goals on electrification.

On Friday there was a dramatic intervention by African ministers early on in the day, with one saying: “We didn’t come here to beg.” Civil society groups, who have a mandated role at the talks, declared it the “worst Cop ever”, with none of their priorities making it through the negotiations. They were particularly frustrated by a failure to take forward a just transition mechanism agreed last year, which they hoped would embed social, racial and economic justice into a low-carbon future.
Related: Cop31 draft climate text dissected: what it says and what it means

Several Cop insiders said Saudi Arabia was one of the countries playing an obstructive role. The petrostate has gained a reputation over the decades for using the Cop process to slow action. Saudi Arabia is understood to be among the countries pushing for carbon capture utilisation and storage (CCUS) to be strongly referenced in the final agreement as a way to help the planet to minimise overshooting the 1.5C temperature goal agreed in Paris.

Neil Grant, a senior expert on mitigation at the advisory group Climate Analytics, said CCUS was being put into the text “because the fossil fuel interests want it in there”. He said: “It’s a Trojan horse for fossil fuel interests.”

Eight countries called for reference to “a clear transition away from fossil fuels” to be restored into the text of any agreement. Panama, Belgium, Côte d’Ivoire, Finland, Greece, the Solomon Islands and Sweden outlined vital issues they said must be addressed, including ensuring polluting countries paid into funds for developing countries to adapt to the climate crisis.

Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama’s climate minister, said: “It is not acceptable to have a Cop or a cover document that does not even mention fossil fuels, and we simply will not put up with it. We need to tell the truth and to speak clearly.”
Panama had sent an open letter to the president of the negotiations, Australian climate change minister Chris Bowen, with a list of demands the country said were not negotiable.

“Well, red lines – that’s how negotiations work,” said Bowen. On Friday afternoon, he said: “There is still a spirit of making it work. People have strong views, of course. I’m not stepping away from that. But no one has said to me, let’s give up and go home.”

In a dramatic press conference on Friday morning, African ministers from Ghana, Zambia, Senegal, Kenya and Sierra Leone said African people were being asked to pay for a crisis they did not cause. They accused rich countries of simultaneously attempting a third exploitation of the continent – after slavery and colonialism – by using carbon taxes to prevent Africans from making use of their wealth of critical minerals to industrialise.

Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings of Ghana, who was ministerial chair of the African group of negotiators, said: “The continent will not accept an outcome that offers declarations without the resources to deliver them. We didn’t come here to beg. We came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries, that they are now being asked to pay for in ways that they never asked.”
A vital request of African nations was for discussion of climate finance. All week civil society observers have accused richer countries, led by the EU, of obstructing progress in talks on money.

The chief climate negotiator for Europe said on Friday that it was already the world leading climate finance donor. A senior EU official said: “We, together with the EU member states, are providing €32.3bn [£27bn] from public sources and mobilising €9.3bn in private finance in 2025 to support developing countries. We’re doing by far the most.”
The last Cop meeting to finish on time was in Italy in 2003. Some talks have dragged into the Sunday after the scheduled Friday finish.

title_en: A Texas Police Department Got $100K After a Single Immigration Arrest. It Stands to Earn Much More.
excerpt_en: The post A Texas Police Department Got $100K After a Single Immigration Arrest. It Stands to Earn Much More. appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: Glenn Harvey for ProPublica and The Texas Tribune Last spring, the police chief in a tiny North Texas suburb called Pantego went before his town council with what might have sounded like an audacious pitch to bring in more money for policing.
His department could accept the federal government’s offer to get into the business of immigration enforcement.

“I won’t say there’s unlimited funding, but there’s quite a bit of money in the fund,” Pantego Police Chief Robert Rife said during the April meeting in which council members approved an agreement with Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
He was right. After a single immigration arrest this past June, Pantego received $100,000.

Rife predicted in his presentation to the council that federal grants could bring in an additional $720,000 for the 2,500-resident town a few miles east of Fort Worth. For perspective, combined with the money it had already received, that’s roughly equivalent to 40% of the town’s $2.1 million police budget last year.

Pantego is one of 429 law enforcement agencies in the state as of mid-September that have entered into agreements with ICE as part of President Donald Trump’s efforts to accelerate deportations. Texas leads the nation in these partnerships, known as 287(g) agreements, which authorize local officers to make immigration arrests during their normal course of duty. A key incentive for local governments across the country has long been the funding that comes with participation.

The federal program funnels millions of dollars to local law enforcement while requiring few measurable results and little tracking of how the money is spent. KXAN reviewed minutes from nine local government meetings and found that, over and over again, Texas law enforcement officials sold the program to their local elected leaders as a boon for their cash-strapped departments.

The same month Pantego decided to join the program, for example, the police chief in the small suburb of Hollywood Park near San Antonio made a similar pitch to his city council. The city “actively profits on payroll for the time spent,” he said.

And in Smith County in East Texas, Sheriff Larry Smith told county commissioners that “equipment, use of fuel, mileage and things of that nature” could all be reimbursed, plus there would be $100,000 for two new vehicles and money for overtime.
“How often do the feds offer us money for anything?” Smith County Commissioner John Moore asked.
“Not very often,” the sheriff responded. He declined to speak with KXAN.

Austin-based immigration attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch worries that local law enforcement will become dependent on the financial incentives, making it difficult to pull away from the program in the future.
“I’m concerned about what this money is going to be doing to the mindset of these small police departments,” she said.
In the Texas Panhandle, Hartley County Sheriff Chanze Fowler said nearly all the federal funding his department receives supports its regular operations, in addition to immigration work.

The sheriff’s office recorded 54 arrests under 287(g) authority from January to early July, most for minor traffic and vehicle violations, according to records obtained by KXAN. It received more than $205,000 during that time. By this past summer, it had spent about $30,000 on things like wages, extra pay for officers who became 287(g) certified, payroll taxes, retirement funds and “fleet purchases.”
Almost all of the 287(g)-related funds “go towards items needed for our everyday job,” Fowler said.

Other local city and law enforcement officials said the additional funds help officers protect their communities and carry out core duties. ICE did not respond to a request for an interview for this story but instead provided a statement that explained the program. Its website says the program targets dangerous criminal offenders.

Pantego officials have declined to answer KXAN’s questions about the department’s involvement with the program since August, despite repeated attempts to reach the mayor, town council, city manager and police chief by phone, email and in person.
“We are not interested in interviewing at this time,” said City Manager Leslie Galloway, the only official to respond.

Ammon Blair, a senior fellow for the Texas Public Policy Foundation, a conservative think tank that supports the program, acknowledged the money can help departments operating on thin budgets, including helping to pay for overtime. But he said there should be more oversight of how the federal money is spent.

KXAN obtained service agreements between ICE and the Smith County Sheriff’s Office and the police department in Bullard, Texas, a town of about 5,300 people in East Texas. The agreements allow either party to terminate with 60 days’ notice. None indicate that the federal government can reclaim funding if an agreement is terminated.

That was one of the selling points in Pantego. The department could get federal funding and eventually drop out of the program without penalty and keep the equipment already purchased, the police chief told town council members. All it had to do was make at least one immigration arrest.

title_en: Ohio Jobs Program Wants Its Money Back After Company’s Failure to Deliver GMO Salmon
excerpt_en: The post Ohio Jobs Program Wants Its Money Back After Company’s Failure to Deliver GMO Salmon appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: The incomplete AquaBounty site in Pioneer, Ohio, in 2024. The project came with promises of 112 new jobs, plus more resources for schools and infrastructure. John D’Angelo for ProPublica When a biotech company named AquaBounty Technologies announced plans to farm genetically engineered Atlantic salmon at a new plant in Ohio, local and state officials eagerly provided it with incentives. Not long after, the company paused construction and auctioned off “new” and “unused” equipment. Now, the state’s private economic development arm wants its $1 million back.

JobsOhio has requested repayment from AquaBounty by Sunday, according to a company filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The filing also notes that, at the end of September, AquaBounty was down to three employees and $122,255 in cash.

AquaBounty said that its salmon could thrive in indoor freshwater farms and help feed the world. Announced in 2021, the new development in Pioneer, Ohio, was supposed to be its first large-scale production facility.
The project came with promises of 112 new jobs, plus more resources for schools and infrastructure. It was believed to be the largest investment ever in rural Williams County.
But AquaBounty, which had never made a profit over its 30 years in business, faced a tangle of regulatory challenges and pushback from environmentalists.

Locals were also suspicious of how the village mayor’s personal interests were tied up in the project. Among other moves, Pioneer Mayor Ed Kidston bought land that AquaBounty wanted to build on. He then sold it to the company for $1.5 million more than he’d paid.

AquaBounty’s plan was unproven, but, as ProPublica reported last year, the company was buoyed by state and local resources — including the million-dollar grant from JobsOhio. The company received the money in August 2021, according to financial filings, shortly after the project went public.

“Why the state was so eager to promote this industry is really puzzling,” said Sherry Fleming of Williams County Alliance, a grassroots environmental group. While AquaBounty had genetic engineering know-how, she said it seemed to have limited experience in production.

Sherry Fleming, of the grassroots environmental group Williams County Alliance, said, “Why the state was so eager to promote this industry is really puzzling.” Nick Hagen for ProPublica In response to ProPublica’s queries, a press contact for AquaBounty said it shares what it can in its SEC releases and filings, and that it’s still in discussion with JobsOhio over the repayment demand. AquaBounty’s filing said that “there can be no assurance that JobsOhio will agree to any payment schedule or other accommodation.”
“Any collection or legal action by JobsOhio could result in additional costs and management distraction,” it added.

Kidston didn’t respond to requests for comment. He said at the time that his actions involving the plant were intended only to help the community. The village administrator referred ProPublica to AquaBounty and its website.

JobsOhio operates privately but has a funding mechanism set up by the state and a board appointed by the governor. Matt Englehart, a spokesperson for JobsOhio, said in an email to ProPublica that it “operates with transparency and accountability,” but its limited disclosures have long been a sore point for Ohioans.

On its website, JobsOhio says its funding model for specialized grants is “independent” and accommodating of “unique needs.” Qualifications include, but aren’t limited to, “job creation, additional payroll, fixed-asset investment commitment, project return on investment, and project location.”

The AquaBounty grant depended on not only the creation of jobs, but also $222 million in capital investment and a payroll of more than $5.4 million by the end of 2026. It had to maintain those commitments through the end of 2028.
Less than two years after it got the money, construction stalled. Roughly 30% built, the site languished at the end of Kexon Drive, a smooth new road that Pioneer had extended for its benefit.

AquaBounty sold equipment intended for the Ohio farm in 2024 and 2025. It also sold its intellectual property for genetically engineered salmon. By the end of September, according to its filing, its primary remaining assets were unsold equipment, the land in Pioneer and the incomplete build.

JobsOhio and other economic development boosters should “take a good look at this because they’re putting taxpayer dollars at risk when they advertise to bring these industries in, and they haven’t done their homework to protect the community,” Fleming said. (JobsOhio is funded by profits from state-controlled liquor sales, not by taxes.)

Englehart told ProPublica that he can’t discuss a situation that may result in litigation. But with any company, he said, “when metric commitments are not met, we work closely with those businesses” to help them overcome challenges.

The One That Got Away: This Small Town Is Left in Limbo After Betting Big on GMO Salmon If all options are exhausted, he added, “we will claw back some or all of our dollars so they can be used for future economic development projects to benefit Ohioans.”

JobsOhio’s demand notice came in September, the financial filing said, informing the company that its equipment sales and consideration of acquisition offers for the Ohio farm were a breach of the grant agreement.

AquaBounty “provided additional information” to JobsOhio in October, the filing said, but the agency upheld its demand and requested repayment this month. If it doesn’t come, the filing said, JobsOhio may refer the matter for collections and “pursue the remedies available” under the grant agreement.

title_en: UK operation wards off risk of cyber-attack on supermarket fridges and freezers
excerpt_en: News of vulnerability comes after retailers in at least seven European countries hit by cyber-attacks
body_en: A secret government cybersecurity operation recently warded off the risk of a cyber-attack on fridges and freezers in UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums, it has emerged.

An attack would have been similar to those that have caused many millions of euros of damage in continental Europe in recent months. But, while many retailers have now been protected, researchers warned that many more could still be vulnerable.
News of the operation led by Whitehall and the National Cyber Security Centre, first reported by the BBC, follows a cyberattack this month of supermarket chains in at least seven European countries.

Another wave of attacks also affected hundreds of retailers across France in October in an act of “unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggression” for which Paris has publicly blamed Iran. The Pentagon is also investigating a suspected hack after a series of fridge malfunctions hit at least six US military bases in August.
Related: The French fridge hacks were relatively unsophisticated. An AI-enabled attack would raise the stakes
Experts told the Guardian that if the vulnerability in UK-based devices had been discovered and exploited before a fix was found, the consequences would have been serious.

“This incident should serve as a wake-up call for the entire refrigeration industry,” said Garry Turner-Smith of Omega Solutions, a refrigeration consultancy firm whose employee, Neil McCourt, found the vulnerability in devices manufactured by Resource Data Management (RDM).

He said: “Had these weaknesses been discovered and exploited by someone with malicious intentions, they could have gained full control of vulnerable RDM data managers and used that access to interfere with refrigeration systems across multiple sites. This raises the prospect of attacks similar to those seen in Europe.”
After Omega was alerted to the weakness, the firm called in the cybersecurity consultants Pen Test Partners to investigate. Both firms then raised their concerns with the manufacturer, RDM.

Ken Munro, Pen Test Partners’ managing partner, said: “We determined that there was an urgent requirement to alert supermarkets and the food supply chain to the issue and fix. “However, we also had to work quietly to avoid alerting less ethical hackers and nation states of the likes of Iran, who are active in this space.”
Munro was attending a retail industry cyber event the day the vulnerabilities were found, enabling him to meet National Cyber Security Centre representatives in person to share the intelligence.

That triggered a series of briefing calls between retailers and officials from the National Cyber Security Centre, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs and the Food Standards Agency, among others, Munro said.
Related: Who is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why?

He added that Pen Test Partners had also tried to alert the owners of exposed devices. “Some controllers were easy to identify and thus contact the owners, but many thousands at small stores are still exposed,” he said.

“The vulnerability is not easy to find for a number of reasons, but once the method is known, it’s easy to recreate. We have not published that method, so there is still time for small operators to take their controllers off the public internet and/or apply the updated firmware.”

A National Cyber Security Centre spokesperson said it had “shared important insight and security advice to ensure that organisations understood potential risks to their networks, and were taking the appropriate measures to mitigate them”.

RDM did not respond to a request for comment. Its chief executive, Ged Evans, told the BBC the vulnerability was “identified in a test environment” that “went beyond” what such exercises usually involved as it “included dismantling our hardware”.

Evans saidd: “In any event we have acted at pace to address this issue and have already deployed first patch releases and have been in proactive contact with our customers to flag any issues and recommend mitigatory steps.”

title_en: How SNAP Theft Happens — and What to Do if It Happens to You
excerpt_en: The post How SNAP Theft Happens — and What to Do if It Happens to You appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: María Jesús Contreras for ProPublica When Kelly Joly swiped her electronic benefits transfer card at a Kroger in Beaumont, Texas, this August, she was trying to buy groceries for herself and her teenage son. Joly had worked for decades as a waitress. The day before her grocery run, she’d received her monthly $530 in Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or food stamp, benefits, she said. But now, her EBT card was being declined. She tried swiping again and began to cry. The cashier told her that this had been happening a lot recently and suggested she report the issue. Joly stepped to the side and called Texas Health and Human Services as her food sat bagged up on the belt.

The representative at the agency that oversees SNAP in Texas told her there was nothing they could do to replace the funds, Joly recalled. Her benefits were gone, likely stolen by fraudsters. Joly said her account showed transactions from the day before at stores in Illinois, Minnesota and California.
“I don’t understand why they wouldn’t replace [our food assistance] if they can see that it was fraud,” she said. “And on top of that, how am I going to feed me and my son this month?”

Scammers Are Stealing Millions From Food Stamp Recipients. Congress Could Fix It — but Won’t. If you receive SNAP benefits, Joly’s experience may sound all too familiar. Last year alone, more than $470 million was stolen from SNAP recipients by card scammers, affecting about 990,000 households.

ProPublica recently published an investigation into why Congress and the Trump administration have failed to crack down on SNAP theft despite promises to tackle fraud and waste in safety-net programs. As part of this reporting, we gathered detailed accounts from more than 50 people across 18 states who’ve had their benefits stolen in the past five years and reviewed dozens more messages, comments and social media posts from people who said they were targeted.

Many of the victims we heard from had similar questions: How did this happen? How can I prevent it from happening again? Why am I not being reimbursed? And why does it seem like little is being done to prevent these crimes in the first place?

We spoke with dozens of federal prosecutors, Secret Service agents, U.S. Department of Agriculture officials, caseworkers, food security advocates and other experts to help answer these questions for you.

How does SNAP theft happen? Much of this crime is the work of low-level street operatives for transnational criminal organizations who install “skimming” devices on card readers at local grocery stores and bodegas. When you swipe your card, these devices capture your data off the magnetic strip on the back, as well as your PIN. That data is either picked up later or transmitted via Bluetooth to thieves waiting nearby.

Skimming is largely preventable via microchips and tap-to-pay technology, which have been greatly successful in reducing fraud in credit and debit card transactions for over a decade. But efforts to install these chips in EBT cards have moved much more slowly.

In recent years, criminals have also used random number generators, phishing calls and spam texts to steal people’s card information, and they will call state hotlines to try to check your SNAP balance and deposit date. In other instances, corner store owners themselves are in cahoots with these scammers, ringing up fake grocery purchases in exchange for cash. And in at least one prominent case, a federal SNAP employee gave sensitive data to criminals for them to be able to steal benefits.

What can I do to protect my benefits? Unfortunately, due to the government’s inaction, the burden of protecting benefits from being stolen has largely been left up to you, the individual SNAP recipient. And the options are less than ideal.

Phone apps, like ebtEdge or Propel, allow you to keep careful track of your card balance, monitor your transaction history for any suspicious purchases and lock your card when it isn’t in use. These apps may also allow you to change your PIN and block out-of-state or online transactions.
But these aren’t always practical solutions, many victims told us. Remembering new PINs all the time, for example, isn’t easy, especially for older beneficiaries.

Cynthia Clark, a 63-year-old retired special education teacher in Jackson, Tennessee, said she has several health conditions that affect the dexterity of her hands, her vision and at times her speech. After her SNAP benefits were stolen in May, she was advised to lock her card every time she wasn’t using it. But she said her disabilities make using a cellphone incredibly difficult. On more than one occasion, she has locked herself out of her SNAP account trying to access her benefits.
“I was simply unable to do whatever the steps were, no matter how hard I tried,” she said.

Besides card locking and changing PINs, the Secret Service has suggested that people may be able to spot evidence of tampering with card readers at grocery stores. For example, if you look closely at the reader and see a noticeable gap between the keypad and the rest of the device, or if you see that something is blocking the light from under the keys, there may be a skimming device there.

An investigative analyst with the Secret Service removes an overlay from a skimming device they found on a card reader at a convenience store in California. Zaydee Sanchez/ProPublica The inside of the card skimmer Zaydee Sanchez/ProPublica What can I do after my benefits have been stolen? If you’ve had your SNAP benefits stolen, you can report the theft to your state or local social services office — the agency where you applied for SNAP — or to the EBT card customer service line on the back of your card to receive a new card and change your PIN so thieves can’t continue to access your benefits.

title_en: Seth Meyers on Elon Musk saying he’s not Maga: ‘Trump’s closest allies are scrambling to get away’
excerpt_en: Late-night hosts discussed Musk distancing himself from Trump as the president palled around with Putin in China
body_en: Late-night hosts mocked Elon Musk’s claim that he is “not Maga” and Donald Trump ’s cozy summit with Xi Jinping and his “friend” Vladimir Putin.

Seth Meyers After a week of cascading outages and tech failures, “Americans are worried because everything is broken,” said Seth Meyers on Thursday’s Late Night. “But rather than fix it, the Trump team is scapegoating Democrats.”
Speaking on cable news, JD Vance claimed that Congress could fix things “with Democrats in Congress if they set aside the ridiculous obsession with men in women’s sports”.

The transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, tried a similar tactic, arguing that Democrats were too concerned with “what names we use” for a plane’s cockpit to pass funding for infrastructure. “Sorry, what the hell are you talking about?!” Meyers retorted. “I don’t remember Joe Biden making a big announcement about changing the name of cockpit – ‘and another thing, we’re renaming the landing strip. From now on it’s called a gender neutral pubic area.’”
Related: Jimmy Kimmel on Trump’s meeting with Xi and Putin: ‘I guess Darth Vader couldn’t make it’

“Voters hate this,” Meyers noted. “That’s why Republicans got crushed in the midterms. Just this week, Democrats won another Senate seat in Alaska and now Trump’s closest allies are scrambling to get away from him as fast as they can.”

On Thursday, Trump’s former friend and associate Elon Musk distanced himself from the president, saying in an interview that the more than $445m he spent on Republican candidates in the midterm elections was “pretty foolish” and that he was “not Maga”.

“I’m sorry, you’re not Maga? But you said this,” Meyers responded before a clip of Musk at a Trump rally from October 2024, in which he sported a black Maga hat and claimed: “I’m not just Maga, I’m dark, gothic Maga.”
“Sounds like you’re Maga, man!” Meyers laughed.

“That would be like you saying, ‘I like to hew my way through wood with an old-fashioned handsaw’ when we all heard you say this,” he added with the infamous clip of Musk wielding a chainsaw on stage at the 2025 CPAC conference.

Meyers continued: “You spent nearly half a billion on Maga candidates, you spoke at the inauguration, you campaigned with Trump and on top of all that, you were at the White House so often you were basically their Kramer. You even sat in the driveway with Trump while he marveled at all the screens in your stupid car.”
Musk’s defection, however unconvincing, is yet more evidence that “the Trump presidency is a failure”, Meyers concluded, “and now everyone involved is racing for the exits”.

Jimmy Kimmel On Jimmy Kimmel Live!, the host recapped Trump’s chummy summit with the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, in China. “For all the diabolical villainy they had hired in one room, I have to say the atmosphere was pretty relaxed,” Kimmel noted.

“Trump really likes being a part of this trio. There were a lot of photo ops. They even joined arms for a little mall walk together,” he added before a clip of the three leaders walking together down a hallway. “There he is, our Darth Tax Evader, and the emperors who gave him his imperial marching orders.”

Speaking to reporters afterwards, Trump rated his meeting with Putin a 12 out of 10, and Putin said the meeting went better than anyone expected. “How is that possible?” Kimmel fumed. “At this point, what more could Trump possibly give him? Alaska?

“It’s so embarrassing watching him interact with these guys,” he continued. “Russia is our enemy. They don’t like us. They are bombing our allies going on now for almost five years. And look at how he greets him!”
Kimmel then played the clip of Trump greeting “my friend” with a close handshake and “nice to see you”.

“How is that OK with anyone?!” he marveled. “Vladimir Putin is a terrible person. He’s a brutal dictator. He is a murderer. He kills people. He poisons them, he has them shoved out of windows. But I guess that’s all OK because ‘he’s my friend.’
“My God, I mean, even if you voted for this guy, you have to admit he has the worst taste in friends,” he concluded next to a photo of Trump with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

title_en: Was Anthropic’s record US$81 billion listing a vote of confidence in AI – and what’s next?
excerpt_en: Now that Anthropic has become a publicly listed company, the AI industry will come under even more intense scrutiny.
body_en: Anthropic, the artificial intelligence giant behind Claude, has just pulled off the biggest initial public offering (IPO) in history. The company raised US$81 billion by listing on the tech-heavy Nasdaq stock market, beating the previous all-time record of US$75 billion set by SpaceX earlier this year.
Initially set at $US83, Anthropic’s share price soared to US$111 after its debut, briefly nudging the company’s value past US$2 trillion, before falling again as investors took profits.

The blockbuster stock market listing comes at a nervous moment in the AI sector. Investors are increasingly questioning whether the huge sums of money being poured into the AI boom are justified, and many are reducing their exposure to technology stocks.
Adding to this shakiness has been the shock departure of chipmaker Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, following an affair scandal.
Anthropic’s debut certainly sets a benchmark for rival OpenAI, which still plans to go public.
But we shouldn’t mistake investor enthusiasm in one company for a broader vote of confidence in the global AI industry.
What does Anthropic’s performance tell us? One thing we can learn from this week’s result is that there is a huge amount of demand for Anthropic itself.
Strong revenue was one factor. At the end of October, Anthropic’s annualised revenue run rate (an estimate of yearly revenue based on the previous month) was US$81 billion.
But the company’s popularity likely also played a role. Claude is one of the most widely used AI tools around the globe. “ Familiarity bias ” is a well known phenomenon in investing.
Intense demand meant many smaller investors missed out on getting shares ahead of the official listing. Last week, Bloomberg reported the share offering was about six times oversubscribed.
According to the Wall Street Journal, only about 15% of available shares were ultimately allocated to retail investors.

Is Anthropic’s huge valuation justified? Anthropic’s share price closed the day at US$97.17, up 17% from its IPO price, which values the company at US$1.76 trillion. That’s slightly less than where SpaceX landed at the end of its first day, at US$2.1 trillion.

But it’s still a colossal figure, even accounting for the fact that Anthropic beat OpenAI to generating a quarterly operating profit earlier this year (before returning to an operating loss the following quarter).

For Anthropic, like any company, going public should make it easier to raise large amounts of capital. That could be important for a company which has already made about US$900 billion in future spending commitments – mostly on computing infrastructure – between now and 2045.
However, it’s important to look at how these commitments play out in the short and long term.
About half of this spending is due by 2030. The near-term bill over the next 12 months is about US$70 billion, which is manageable with its current revenue run rate of US$81 billion.

Other concerns may be more pressing. Anthropic’s third-quarter revenue rose 47% – which is strong – but this compares to a growth rate of 144% in the second quarter. This suggests a sharp slowdown in growth overall.
Token prices have also been falling, driven in part by more competition from cheaper AI models.

Also on revenue, the company has warned that some of its customers – “particularly early-stage and high-growth companies” – rely on external financing. This could reduce their spending with Anthropic if that financing dries up.
What to watch after this public listing For any company, listing on a public stock exchange introduces much more scrutiny.
Previously, the focus on Anthropic has centred on its technology and growth potential. Now, there’ll be a renewed focus on corporate governance.

Beyond the financial metrics of revenue growth, profitability, cash flow and more, investors will now more closely scrutinise how management balances commercial returns with AI safety, privacy and social responsibility.

title_en: The most iconic sports film of all time taught us winning isn’t everything: 50 years of Rocky
excerpt_en: Rocky’s underdog story is in many ways also Sylvester Stallone’s story.
body_en: IMDB By all measures, Rocky (1976) is the most successful sport film of all time. Half a century on from its release, the story of small-time boxer Rocky Balboa – who rises to square up against heavyweight champion Apollo Creed — continues to capture our imagination.

Directed by John G. Avildsen, the film won the prestigious Best Picture and Best Directing Oscars in 1977. And the broader franchise, consisting of five sequels and three Creed spin-offs, has generated more than US$1 billion at the global box office.

Rocky resonates because it is the ultimate underdog story. The hero is flawed, yet faithful to his dreams – working to overcome his self-doubt. His final victory is not a boxing title, but in proving his worth.
Standing your ground The story of Rocky, written by Sylvester Stallone himself, was inspired by a real-life match between heavy weight champion Muhammad Ali and Chuck Wepner.
Wepner was a little known boxer from New Jersey at the time. While he didn’t win the fight, he held his own, becoming one of few boxers in history to be able to knock Ali down.
for one brief moment, this supposed stumblebum turned out to be magnificent. And he lasted and knocked the champ down. I thought: ‘if this isn’t a metaphor for life.’

Hollywood lore tells how Stallone wrote the script in just three days after seeing Ali and Wepner’s fight. Stallone later admitted that 90% of this original script was terrible, but the “germ of the idea was there”. He says it took about 25 rewrites to get it right.
When interested producers wanted a famous name to take on the eponymous role, Stallone declined. He was determined to play Rocky.

It was a big risk, since Stallone was broke – so broke he was forced to sell his dog, Butkus, for US$40. But like Rocky he had faith in himself, and persisted until the studio, United Artists, agreed to cast him in the role.
When paid his advance, Stallone was able to buy Butkus back for $15,000. The hound went on to feature in several Rocky films.
Butkus, Stallone’s bullmastiff, died in 1981 from a heart attack. IMDB Rocky was filmed on a budget of just US$1 million, a small budget for a film, even in those days.
Many of the scenes were shot in public, including those in the famous training montage, in which curious members of the public watch on as Rocky jogs through the streets.
In one unscripted moment, a street seller throws Rocky an orange as he jogs past. This detail adds charm to the scene, instilling the sense of Rocky as the everyday man.
The training montage also doubles as a metaphor for the American dream, which promises that hard work and persistence will lead to success.
Such montages have since become commonplace in sports films, from Karate Kid (1984) to Million Dollar Baby (2004). But Stallone is often credited as having pioneered the format.
Rocky represents a powerful ethos There has been much discussion about just what Rocky captured in the American psyche that led to its success.

Rocky wasn’t simply a fairytale about the American dream, although this was part of it. The film reflected the neglected working class at a time of growing “ethnic” pride – and local audiences connected with this.
The film’s global success, however, arguably comes down to its core message: recognition of the self.
As film academic Eric Lichtenfeld argues, Rocky is not just training to become a better boxer – he is searching for respect, both internally and externally.
By taking on Apollo Creed, and proving himself to be a worthy opponent, he demonstrates his worth in the world – even if he doesn’t win the final fight.
The appeal of this kind of underdog story transcends cultural boundaries.
It also goes to the heart of sport, as we’ve seen with Olympians like Eddy the Eagle and Eric the Eel.
